items.content_html:
fetch_indexes, fetch_foreign_keys, fetch_check_constraints, fetch_unique_constraints and fetch_exclusion_constraints matched an unqualified name against every schema on the search path, so a name two schemas both carry came back with both tables' indexes and constraints.

fetch_primary_keys and fetch_table_options already resolved such a name the way ::regclass does. Their DISTINCT ON (relname) subquery is now a WITH tables CTE built by resolved_tables, and every reader joins against it rather than filtering on relname and nspname itself.
items.title: Read PostgreSQL indexes and constraints from the table a name resolves to

items.content_html:
The CALLBACKS constant has been outdated for a long time, and is only referenced in tests. It is missing several transaction related callbacks that have been added over the years:

  • before_commit
  • after_save_commit
  • after_create_commit
  • after_update_commit
  • after_destroy_commit

Anything driven off the constant silently skips those callbacks, so it is deprecated with no replacement, and will be removed in Rails 9.0.
items.title: Deprecate `ActiveRecord::Callbacks::CALLBACKS`

items.content_html:
rails new --database=mysql scanned a hardcoded list of socket paths and, when one of them existed, wrote socket: into config/database.yml instead of host:. The list dates back to 2008 and still named MacPorts' mysql4 and mysql5 ports, neither of which resolves on a current machine.

Baking the generating machine's socket path into a committed file is also at odds with Docker and devcontainers, so the generated configuration now always uses host:, which DB_HOST already overrides. That drops the !devcontainer? guard from the templates too.
items.title: Stop probing for a local MySQL socket when generating `config/database.yml`

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

TestHelpersTests::GenerationTest#test_build_app_after_tmp_path_is_removed fails on main with an environment leak reported by the LeakChecker added in 64aa7ee.

Detail

$ cd railties
$ bundle exec ruby -Itest test/isolation/test_helpers_test.rb -i test_build_app_after_tmp_path_is_removed
  1) Failure:
TestHelpersTests::GenerationTest#test_build_app_after_tmp_path_is_removed [tools/support/leak_checker.rb:54]:
Environment leak detected:
  - Added variables:
    - RAILS_ENV

1 runs, 3 assertions, 1 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips

build_app saved the previous value with @prev_rails_env ||= ENV["RAILS_ENV"] before setting ENV["RAILS_ENV"] = "development".

When RAILS_ENV is unset, the captured value is nil, so ||= re-captures on every call. That test calls build_app twice without a teardown_app in between, so the second call recorded the "development" value the first call had just set. teardown_app then restored "development" instead of deleting the variable, and RAILS_ENV leaked out of the test.

Capturing with unless defined?(@prev_rails_env) records the original value exactly once, so teardown_app deletes RAILS_ENV as it should when it was unset to begin with.

This Pull Request has been created because rate_limit only applies via a before_action, evaluated before the action runs. Some rate limits can only be decided once the action is executing, e.g. counting failed login attempts rather than every attempt.

It gains its own defaults (matching rate_limit's) so it can be called with just to:/within:. Documentation was added on #rate_limiting, including a login-rate-limiting example, and cross-referenced from rate_limit with guidance on when to use which method. Tests covering the in-action usage were added.

Additional information

rate_limit remains the right choice for limiting one or more actions wholesale; rate_limiting is for when the decision depends on logic inside the action.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

#55583 added @is_utc = zone == "UTC" || zone == "UCT" to ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone#initialize so that #xmlschema and #to_s could take a fast path for UTC instances. #zone goes through #period, which resolves the TZInfo::TimezonePeriod, so since 8.1 every TimeWithZone instantiation performs a period lookup even when nothing ever needs it. Before that the lookup was lazy; the test asserting @period stays nil after construction was removed in the same PR.

That sits under Time.zone.now, Time#in_time_zone, TimeWithZone#+/#-/#since/#ago/#change, and Active Record time attribute casting. Compared to 8.0, instantiation went from 1 allocation to 5 and got 3–10x slower.

Detail

The first commit makes the check lazy. @is_utc starts as nil and is computed and memoized on the first #utc? call; #xmlschema and #to_s call #utc? instead of reading the ivar. #utc? joins the #freeze preload list so frozen instances don't raise. The removed test is restored. The formatting fast paths keep their gains because they need the period anyway outside UTC.

The second commit goes one step further for zones that are always UTC, which is the default Time.zone. Every zone in tzdata whose abbreviation is UTC/UCT (Etc/UTC, Etc/UCT, Etc/Universal, Etc/Zulu and their links) is a constant-offset zone with no transitions, so ActiveSupport::TimeZone computes an always-UTC flag at construction by checking that its period has neither a start nor an end transition and a UTC abbreviation. TimeWithZone#utc? short-circuits on that flag and only falls back to the period-based check otherwise, so the semantics are unchanged for every other zone. Time.zone.now.iso8601/.as_json/.to_s under UTC no longer touch TZInfo at all. The fallback to the period-based check is kept for custom tzinfo objects; no zone in tzdata reaches it, which I verified over every identifier under both the zoneinfo and tzinfo-data data sources.

Two duck-typing contracts get slightly tighter: TimeWithZone.new now needs a zone that responds to utc?, and TimeZone.create(name, offset, tzinfo) now calls period_for_utc and reads start_transition/end_transition at construction. Nothing in Rails or the test suite passes anything but ActiveSupport::TimeZone and TZInfo::Timezone there.

Additional information

Ruby 4.0.6 +PRISM, benchmark-ips, Time.zone = "Eastern Time (US & Canada)", iterations per second and allocations per call, 8.0 -> main -> this PR:

TWZ.new(utc, zone)      7.92M -> 731k -> 7.85M   1 -> 5 -> 1
Time.zone.now           2.16M -> 563k -> 2.33M   2 -> 6 -> 2
Time#in_time_zone       3.77M -> 655k -> 3.71M   1 -> 5 -> 1
twz + 1                 2.45M -> 590k -> 2.44M   2 -> 6 -> 2
TWZ.new(..).to_i        6.25M -> 712k -> 6.11M   1 -> 5 -> 1
twz.xmlschema           1.08M -> 3.40M -> 3.36M  4 -> 2 -> 2
TWZ.new(..).xmlschema   413k -> 605k -> 595k     10 -> 7 -> 7
TWZ.new(..).to_s        422k -> 497k -> 490k     11 -> 7 -> 7

Time.zone = "UTC", main -> first commit -> both commits:

TWZ.new(..).utc?               1.07M -> 1.06M -> 6.00M   5 -> 5 -> 1
Time.zone.now.iso8601          686k -> 692k -> 1.76M     7 -> 7 -> 3
Time.zone.now.to_s             584k -> 575k -> 1.17M     8 -> 7 -> 3
Time.zone.now.as_json          650k -> 657k -> 1.58M     7 -> 7 -> 3
now.in_time_zone(UTC).iso8601  842k -> 833k -> 2.54M     6 -> 6 -> 2

Outside UTC, instantiate-then-format is within noise of main (the extra utc? dispatch costs a few percent on TWZ.new(..).xmlschema, 605k vs 577–595k across runs); formatting an existing instance is unchanged.

Benchmark script:

require "benchmark/ips"
require "active_support"
require "active_support/time"

Time.zone = "Eastern Time (US & Canada)"
ZONE = Time.zone
NOW = Time.now.utc
TWZ = ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone.new(NOW, ZONE)

def allocs(n = 1000)
  yield
  GC.disable
  before = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
  n.times { yield }
  after = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
  GC.enable
  ((after - before).to_f / n).round(1)
end

CASES = {
  "TWZ.new(utc, zone)"     => -> { ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone.new(NOW, ZONE) },
  "Time.zone.now"          => -> { Time.zone.now },
  "Time#in_time_zone"      => -> { NOW.in_time_zone(ZONE) },
  "twz + 1"                => -> { TWZ + 1 },
  "TWZ.new(..).to_i"       => -> { ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone.new(NOW, ZONE).to_i },
  "twz.xmlschema"          => -> { TWZ.xmlschema },
  "TWZ.new(..).xmlschema"  => -> { ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone.new(NOW, ZONE).xmlschema },
  "TWZ.new(..).to_s"       => -> { ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone.new(NOW, ZONE).to_s },
}

CASES.each { |name, blk| printf "%-24s %5.1f objs\n", name, allocs(&blk) }
Benchmark.ips do |x|
  CASES.each { |name, blk| x.report(name, &blk) }
end

The regression shipped in 8.1.0. The first commit is the backport candidate, though its #xmlschema/#to_s hunks are written against #58751 (main only) and will need a separate rebase for 8-1-stable. The second commit adds TimeZone#utc? and is main-only.
items.title: Avoid eager period lookup in TimeWithZone#initialize

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

ActiveRecord::Inheritance::ClassMethods#find_sti_class guards the resolved class with descendants.include?(subclass). descendants is not memoized: every call walks Class#subclasses recursively, allocating two arrays per node, and the result is then scanned linearly. This runs once per record for every STI model that is instantiated — from find, instantiate and subclass_from_attributes alike — so the cost scales with rows × subclasses.

On an application with an STI base class of 46 subclasses and ~45 such rows per request, this guard alone was ~28% of request CPU and half of all allocations in a production-shaped profile.

Detail

This Pull Request replaces descendants.include?(subclass) with subclass < self.

For classes, subclass < self is true exactly when self is among subclass.ancestors, which is the same relation a transitive walk of Class#subclasses from self computes. sti_class_for only ever returns a class currently bound to a constant, so the reloading filter that descendants applies (DescendantsTracker.reject!) cannot change the answer: a class removed by the reloader is never returned by constantize/compute_type, and a stale self has no live descendants under either check. Behaviour and the SubclassNotFound message are unchanged; the new check walks the ancestor chain and allocates nothing.

A test asserts the lookup no longer calls descendants for a direct child, a grandchild, a great-grandchild and an unrelated class; the existing SubclassNotFound tests keep covering the raise paths.

Additional information

Micro-benchmark on the test suite's Company hierarchy (15 descendants), 20 000 × Company.instantiate("id" => 1, "type" => "VerySpecialClient"), Ruby 4.0.5:

old   12.80 us/instantiate   62 alloc/instantiate
new    4.64 us/instantiate   14 alloc/instantiate

The guard itself on a 46-subclass base class: descendants.include? 14.44 µs / 141 allocations → subclass < self 0.02 µs / 0 allocations.

I could not find an existing issue or PR for this; main still carries the descendants.include? check. The .new fast path in 3295ff9 is the closest prior change to this method.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

ACLs-disabled ("bucket owner enforced") is now both the default and the Controlling ownership of objects and disabling ACLs for your bucket object ownership setting for S3 buckets.

Bucket owner enforced (default) – ACLs are disabled, and the bucket owner automatically owns and has full control over every object in the bucket. ACLs no longer affect permissions to data in the S3 bucket. The bucket uses policies to define access control.

Yet ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service unconditionally sets the public-read ACL on every upload for services configured with public: true:

@upload_options[:acl] = "public-read" if public?

On a bucket using this default, recommended setting, ACLs are disabled entirely, so any PUT request carrying an ACL header is rejected with AccessControlListNotSupported. As of today, an application targeting such a bucket has no way to opt out of this ACL.

Detail

Change ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service to introduce config.active_storage.s3_public_uploads_via_acl:

  • Defaults to true. No behavior change for any existing application.
  • New applications generated with config.load_defaults 8.2 get false.
  • When false, S3Service no longer sets the ACL; the app is expected to grant public read access through a bucket policy instead. Buckets that still use ACLs can restore the previous behavior for a given service by setting the acl option explicitly in its upload section of the service configuration.

items.content_html:
Summary

Fixes #48787.

When calling logger.tagged(*tags) without a block, ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging returns a new logger with the tags applied as instance/local tags.

Previously, LocalTagStorage implemented this by defining attr_accessor :tag_stack on the formatter instance, storing tags in an instance variable (@tag_stack = TagStack.new). Because @tag_stack was an instance variable on the formatter rather than stored in IsolatedExecutionState, it was shared across all threads using that formatter. Consequently:

  • Any block-scoped tagging (e.g. logger.tagged("Job") { ... }) on such a logger mutated the shared @tag_stack, causing tags from one thread to leak into concurrent threads or nested threads.
  • push_tags, pop_tags, and clear_tags! operations on the logger mutated the shared instance variable across threads.
  • Cloned formatters inherited the memoized @thread_key from the original formatter, causing different formatters to share execution state.

Solution

  1. In LocalTagStorage, store instance-level tags separately in @local_tags (precomputing @local_tags_string for fast formatting) instead of replacing tag_stack.
  2. Keep tag_stack backed by IsolatedExecutionState, ensuring that all dynamic/block-scoped tagging and push/pop operations remain isolated per thread/fiber.
  3. Update Formatter#call and Formatter#tags_text to format both @local_tags and tag_stack.tags.
  4. Reset @thread_key = nil in Formatter#initialize_clone and Formatter#initialize_dup so cloned formatters receive distinct execution state keys.
  5. In TaggedLogging#initialize_clone and TaggedLogging#initialize_dup, ensure the formatter is also cloned/duped.
items.title: Fix thread isolation for TaggedLogging instances created without block

items.content_html:
Summary

Fixes #42802.

Integer division of a duration (e.g. 1.hour / 10) truncates parts to integers, and zero parts are dropped during initialization. That leaves a duration with an empty parts hash but a non-zero value (360 seconds). When such a duration is added to another, the merge logic only looked at parts, so those seconds were lost from both parts and inspect output.

This change treats empty parts as { seconds: value } when merging durations in Duration#+, Duration::Scalar#+, and Duration::Scalar#-.

Before / After

(1.second + 1.hour / 10).inspect
# Before: "1 second"
# After:  "361 seconds"

(1.second + 1.hour / 10).parts
# Before: { seconds: 1 }
# After:  { seconds: 361 }

Test plan

  • Repro script: ruby -I../rails/activesupport/lib duration_inspect_42802_test.rb
  • cd activesupport && bin/test test/core_ext/duration_test.rb (86 runs, 0 failures)
items.title: Fix #42802: Duration#inspect after integer division

items.content_html:
Deals with errors such as @serialize_cast_value_compatible from ActiveRecord::Type::DateTime

serialize_cast_value_compatible? memoizes into a class ivar. The eager compute in #initialize normally keeps that write on main, but ActiveRecord::Type::TypeMap builds types lazily, so a column first touched inside a Ractor raises straight out of #initialize. The other reacher, .serialize, has an inline rescue nil that swallows the IsolationError and leaves the type on #serialize for the rest of the process.

This proxies only the first write through ActiveSupport::Ractors.on_main, keeping the defined? read as the fast path: false is a legitimate memo value, so the guard cannot become ||=. Three tests, all failing without it.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #57822.

Mailgun inbound email webhooks send the entire raw RFC 822 email payload (including attachments) in a URL-encoded form parameter named body-mime with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

In Rack 3, Rack::QueryParser enforces a default bytesize_limit of 4 MB (4194304 bytes). When an incoming email exceeds 4 MB, Rack raises Rack::QueryParser::QueryLimitError, which Rails converts into ActionController::BadRequest. The request is rejected before Action Mailbox can process the email.

Detail

This Pull Request resolves the issue by introducing a scoped request parser middleware specifically for the Mailgun ingress:

  1. ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::RequestParser:

    • Only intercepts POST requests to /rails/action_mailbox/mailgun/inbound_emails/mime with application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
    • Performs a bounded read of the input stream up to @bytesize_limit + 2 bytes (preserving Rack's memory protection semantics).
    • Parses query pairs using a dedicated Rack::QueryParser configured with @bytesize_limit.
    • Pre-populates env["rack.request.form_pairs"] and env["rack.request.form_vars"], preventing downstream middleware or controller parameter parsing from re-evaluating the body against Rack's global 4 MB limit.

  2. Configuration:

    • Adds config.action_mailbox.mailgun_payload_size_limit, defaulting to 25.megabytes.
    • Inserts the middleware via insert_after Rack::Runtime, which:
      • Safely precedes Rack::MethodOverride in standard applications.
      • Operates cleanly in API-only applications (config.api_only = true) where Rack::Runtime is present.
      • Preserves default middleware order, unshift semantics, and host authorization protection.

  3. Documentation and Tests:

    • Documented config.action_mailbox.mailgun_payload_size_limit in guides/source/configuring.md.
    • Added unit tests for RequestParser verifying bounded reads, limit enforcement, and isolation from unrelated endpoints.
    • Added integration test verifying large Mailgun payloads (> 4 MB) are accepted by the ingress endpoint.
    • Added Railties middleware tests verifying custom limit configuration and API-only boot compatibility.
    • Added CHANGELOG entry in actionmailbox/CHANGELOG.md.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58732.

The Associations Guide and Active Record documentation explain that build_association returns a new, unsaved object for a has_one association. However, they do not make clear that building this object replaces the association's current target and may immediately modify, nullify, or destroy an existing persisted record.

This behavior is particularly surprising with dependent: :destroy, where calling build_association on a persisted owner destroys the existing target before the newly built object is saved.

Detail

This Pull Request clarifies the has_one saving and replacement behavior in both the Active Record API documentation and the Associations Guide:

  • In activerecord/lib/active_record/associations.rb:
    • Updated the Auto-saving overview to note that replaced objects will still be removed or saved to update foreign keys according to the association's :dependent option.
    • Explicitly documented in build_association that an existing associated record is immediately removed or destroyed according to the :dependent option.
  • In guides/source/association_basics.md:
    • Added a warning callout in section 2.6 clarifying that while the newly built object remains unsaved, building it replaces the current target and immediately removes or destroys any existing persisted target according to :dependent.

items.content_html:
Since #58060, a Ractor built its notifier from a snapshot of the subscriptions taken on first use and never looked at it again, so subscriptions added or removed later were invisible to it. The snapshot was also assembled outside Fanout's mutex.

Replace Fanout's Concurrent::Map / Array pair with Fanout::Registry, which subscribe / unsubscribe replace instead of mutating in place. A Ractor compares identity to tell that the registry it materialized went stale, and adopts the new one.

cc @gmcgibbon @Edouard-chin
items.title: Make notification subscriptions an immutable registry

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58292.

extract_value_from_default returned actual Ruby true / false objects for DEFAULT TRUE / DEFAULT FALSE literals, unlike every other branch in that method, which returns a String.

This pre-cast value became the attribute's value_before_type_cast, so overriding a boolean column with:

attribute :name, :integer

fed a Ruby boolean directly into Integer#deserialize, raising:

NoMethodError: undefined method `to_i' for true

This is a residual gap in fb04401a66 ("Stop deserializing column defaults"), which fixed the general column-default double-casting issue behind #58292 but reintroduced the same failure specifically for SQLite's TRUE / FALSE literal parsing.

Detail

This Pull Request changes SQLite boolean default extraction to return "1" / "0" strings instead of Ruby true / false objects.

This matches the plain-scalar contract of the other branches in extract_value_from_default and restores the pre-8.1 behavior where the column default round-trips through the overriding type correctly.

Regression coverage verifies that:

  • a boolean schema default can be read through an overridden integer attribute type; and
  • a non-boolean integer value can still be written and reloaded through the overridden attribute.

Additional information

MySQL / Trilogy already return plain numeric strings for tinyint(1) defaults and are unaffected by this regression.

PostgreSQL already returns the literal "true" / "false" string, rather than a cast Ruby Boolean, from its own extract_value_from_default, so it is not affected by this particular regression.

PostgreSQL has separate, longstanding limitations with overriding native boolean columns with non-boolean attribute types. Those behaviors predate this regression and are outside the scope of this change.

items.content_html:
The Asset Pipeline guide's migration steps listed config/assets.rb and assets/config/manifest.js, but the actual paths are config/initializers/assets.rb and app/assets/config/manifest.js, per propshaft's UPGRADING.md.

Motivation / Background

The Asset Pipeline guide's "Migration Steps" section (step 2) tells readers to delete config/assets.rb and assets/config/manifest.js. Neither path matches where these files actually live in a Rails app, so following the guide literally does nothing.

Detail

This Pull Request corrects the two paths to config/initializers/assets.rb and app/assets/config/manifest.js, matching propshaft's own UPGRADING.md, which lists these deletions separately (step 4 and step 5 in different sections). The guide appears to have dropped the intermediate directories when condensing both steps into one line.

Additional information

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Rich text holding a content attachment (<action-text-attachment content-type="text/html" content="…">) can't be rendered from a namespaced controller, from a non-HTML request, or outside a request. ActionText::Attachables::ContentAttachment#to_html hands the ActionText::Content object to the renderer, so Action View resolves it as an object partial:

  • From Admin::MessagesController, prefix_partial_path_with_controller_namespace turns action_text/contents/content into admin/action_text/contents/_content, which doesn't exist: ActionView::MissingTemplate.
  • From a JSON request, the lookup is restricted to formats: [:json], so the HTML partial isn't found either. (Top-level content passes formats: :html explicitly; the nested render doesn't.)
  • From a job, there's no controller renderer, so Action Text falls back to Class.new(ActionController::Base).renderer, whose prefix is nil, and merge_prefix_into_object_path raises undefined method 'include?' for nil.

We hit all three in production this evening: a comment with a content attachment 500'd the create request from a namespaced comments controller and then failed every webhook delivery job for that event.

Detail

Render the content partial by path with formats: :html, the same way ActionText::Content#to_rendered_html_with_layout renders top-level content. Adds tests for the namespaced controller, the JSON request, and the job, each of which raises without the change.

Checklist

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why.
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries.
